The body. Learn these words with your hands on them:

ḻiya → head
buku → forehead, face
maṉutji → eye
buthuru → ear
matha → tongue, language (yes, the same word, Yolŋu Matha, the Yolŋu tongue!)
dhä → mouth (remember dhä'yun, to open the mouth, and dhäŋuru, after, from-the-end?)
goṉ → hand, arm
ḻuku → foot (and ḻukuy marrtji, going by foot, Lesson 11!)
diltji → back (and listen for its near-twin ḏiltji, retroflex ḏ, the bush, the back-country, the land's own back)
guḻun → stomach, belly
ŋayaŋu → feelings, the inner self

Now, three things the body does in this grammar:

1. The body builds the language's imagery.
Body parts are the favourite first half of compound words (Lesson 16's logic, made flesh):
ḻiya-ḏäl → head-hard → clever, determined
gandarr-ḏumurru → belly-big → fat
buthuru-bitjun → to ear-do → to listen, to heed
Bili nhe buthuru-bitjurruna? → Have you heard? (Did you ear-it?)

Mind, character, attention, all located in the body. Not metaphorically located: grammatically located.

2. Your body doesn't need my/your.
When you wash, hit, or hurt a body part, and it's YOURS, the possessive usually stays silent. Whose head would you be washing? The part sits next to the verb, plainly, and the reflexive machinery from Lesson 24 does the ownership work. English insists on I washed MY hands, claiming ownership of your own hands every single time; here the body is not property. It's you. Inalienable, as linguists say: not able to be otherwise-owned.

3. Part and whole sit side by side.
To say the woman's hand or the tree's top, you often don't need possessive suffixes at all, whole and part simply stand together, in agreement (Lesson 36!): remember garrwarŋuru dharpaŋuru, from the top from the tree. The part belongs by adjacency, by shared case, by being of the same body.

And maybe keep this one closest: ŋayaŋu, the feelings, the inside, is a body part in this list. Emotion isn't abstract here, it has an anatomy, it sits in you like a stomach or a tongue. When someone asks after your ŋayaŋu, they're not being poetic. They're being precise.
